newsitem.title: UK: AMERSHAM UP ON NYCOMED RESULTS, INDEX HOPES.
newsitem.headline: AMERSHAM UP ON NYCOMED RESULTS, INDEX HOPES.

text.p: Shares in Amersham International Plc hit a record high on Thursday after its planned merger partner Nycomed ASA pleased investors with first-half profits.
Hopes for the merged company to eventually be included in the FTSE 100 index, widening the investor pool, also boosted the stock, traders and analysts said.
By 1100 GMT, Amersham shares were up 54p at 21.01-1/2 stg, hitting a record 21.05 stg.
"I think what we're really seeing is a recognition of the strategic power of the Nycomed merger," said Alyson Coates, pharmaceuticals analyst at SocGen.
"The Nycomed figures are a bit better than expected but I would characterise them as reassuring," she said.
Nycomed A class shares were up sharply, at 166 crowns, following the release of better-than-expected first-half 1997 profits of 604 million crowns.
The result fell 74 million crowns short of the corresponding 1996 pre-tax profit, but it beat market expectations.
Amersham, the healthcare and technology group, and Nycomed, Norway's largest pharmaceuticals group, announced on July 1 their plan to merge.
The Financial Times said on Thursday that the market capitalisation of Amersham would likely propel the company into the FTSE 100 upon completion of the merger.
An Amersham spokesman had no comment on being included in the FTSE 100 but said the merger was expected to be completed in September or October, pending shareholder approval.
Amersham also announced on June 10 its plans to merge its Life Science division with Pharmacia Biotech.
"There are additional benefits as the size of the combination will widen the investor pool," Coates said. "Bringing it into the index would increase its trade-ability."
At today's share price, with 59.07 million shares, the market capitalisation of Amersham is roughly 1.24 billion sterling.
The companies in the FTSE 100 are reviewed every quarter and the next meeting is September 10, followed by December, said Mark Makepeace, managing director of FTSE International.
All companies in the UK market are ranked by size but a rule is used to prevent too much turnover in the index, he said.
A company outside the index has to have a market capitalisation above the 90th ranking to get in, or below the 110th ranking to fall out of the FTSE 100, Makepeace said.
The two smallest companies in the FTSE 100 as of Wednesday's close were Tate and Lyle Plc, at 1.8 billion sterling, and Imperial Tobacco Group Plc, at 1.98 billion sterling, Makepeace said.
